findings.assertion: The 1922 San Ildefonso mural commissions formed part of the Obregón administration's postrevolutionary education project under José Vasconcelos, who headed the SEP from 10 October 1921 to 28 January 1924. These murals occupied walls of the Escuela Nacional Preparatoria rather than a museum originally built to display them.
findings.source_locator: San Ildefonso acervo lines 40–45; INBAL bulletin 980 'El muralismo a cien años'
findings.limitations: Institutional chronology checked, but original SEP commissioning contracts and student reception not inspected.

findings.assertion: The initial 1922 team at the preparatory school included Rivera, Charlot, Leal, Ramón Alva de la Canal and Revueltas; Siqueiros and Orozco joined later. The collective project also depended on assistants including Xavier Guerrero, Amado de la Cueva, Carlos Mérida and Máximo Pacheco, so a narrative restricted to three famous painters would distort attribution.
findings.source_locator: San Ildefonso exhibition 'Muralistas en San Ildefonso'; INBAL bulletin 980 collaborator paragraph
findings.limitations: Specific contracts, payroll and attribution of each hand on each fresco not independently inspected.

findings.assertion: The revolutionary muralism milieu included women artists and activists—among them Nahui Olin, Graciela Amador, Tina Modotti, and others—and Indigenous artists and models, including Máximo Pacheco and Luz Jiménez. Their roles should not be equated automatically: the exhibition catalog distinguishes models, image-makers, activists and assistants.
findings.source_locator: San Ildefonso 'Mujeres artistas y activistas' and 'Muralistas'; Leal page lines 38–40
findings.limitations: Official exhibition is interpretive synthesis; individual original biographies and contracts not checked. Do not assert all listed women painted the school's walls.

findings.assertion: UNAM quotes a 1923 Escuela Nacional Preparatoria report assigning Orozco work on the main courtyard and Siqueiros on the smaller courtyard staircase, after initial resistance from Vasconcelos. The account describes a contested commission, not a universally harmonious government-sponsored art program.
findings.source_locator: Gaceta UNAM 2022-10-17 lines 12–17, attributed quotation from ENP 1923 report
findings.limitations: Original 1923 report not inspected; conflict described by specialist interviewed in 2022, not directly verified.

findings.assertion: Orozco's San Ildefonso murals underwent interruption and substantial repainting: a UNAM interview reports that he returned in 1926 and destroyed earlier compositions except specified surviving work. Therefore the paintings now visible cannot be assumed to depict all imagery first commissioned in 1923.
findings.source_locator: Gaceta UNAM lines 15–19; San Ildefonso acervo lines 43–45, 83–155
findings.limitations: Chronology and survival depend on interview secondary account; original painted-layer conservation analysis missing.

findings.assertion: The San Ildefonso collection locates Rivera's La Creación (1922) in the Anfiteatro, contrasting with Orozco's 1923–1926 works across the three levels of the main courtyard and stair landing. A guide should assign separate observation stops rather than imply these murals occupy one wall.
findings.source_locator: San Ildefonso acervo lines 43–53, 83–155; exhibition section 'Muralistas'
findings.limitations: Current 2026 room access and conservation closures not confirmed; no visitor route should be published yet.

findings.assertion: Charlot's Masacre en el Templo Mayor and Leal's Los danzantes de Chalma were arranged on opposing walls near the stair. The exhibition interprets them as deliberately dialoguing historical conquest violence and twentieth-century religious practice; the murals are evidence of 1920s historical imagination, NOT eyewitness depiction of 1520.
findings.source_locator: Charlot page lines 3–10; Leal page lines 33–40; exhibition 'Muralistas'
findings.limitations: Interpretation from institution; on-site line-of-sight not checked; do not use mural as archaeological evidence for Mexica rituals.

findings.assertion: On Charlot's massacre mural the college's description identifies a central three-color standard, diagonally advancing Spaniards, and small portraits of Rivera, Leal and Charlot at lower right. These identifiable details provide a concrete looking prompt, but the scene's iconography uses a twentieth-century interpretation of conquest.
findings.source_locator: San Ildefonso Charlot mural page lines 7–10
findings.limitations: Visitor physical access and precise direction of the painting not checked; interpretive attributions are institutional, not primary testimony for colonial events.

findings.assertion: Revueltas's Allegoría de la Virgen de Guadalupe (1922–1923) integrates an image of campesino, Indigenous and Afrodescendant collectivity, and the institution identifies his signature with hammer-and-sickle symbolism and union membership. The material offers an observed entry point into contested religious and class politics after the Revolution.
findings.source_locator: Revueltas catalogue lines 81–93; exhibition paired entrance walls
findings.limitations: Interpretation institutional and not universally accepted; visitors' access and material state not verified.

findings.assertion: The Jean Charlot Collection catalog provides a more precise work chronology—2 October 1922 to 31 January 1923, with a 1 February 1923 inauguration—than the general 1922–1923 label, and separately catalogs scaled composition, geometric plan, cartoons, and a numbered giornate drawing. These are primary-material research leads for mural-making technique, not yet original objects examined.
findings.source_locator: Charlot Collection catalogue lines 2–14 and 21–38; site acervo lines 69–74
findings.limitations: Catalogue metadata direct, but graphic objects and dated supporting documents not inspected. Copyright clearance required before displaying photographs or plans.

findings.assertion: Technique labels across San Ildefonso's own public pages require critical separation: the acervo lists Leal's Chalma work as encaustic, whereas the exhibition page labels it 'Fresco' in a heading while describing encaustic in its body. A future guide should not resolve the medium by simple majority or substitute a simplified 'all fresco' label.
findings.source_locator: Acervo lines 75–80 vs Leal exhibition page lines 33–39; conflicting labels within institutional materials
findings.limitations: No technical materials analysis, conservation report, or historic recipe inspected; retain formal unresolved material attribution.
